name: Braun Silk-expert IPL
lead: Braun Silk·expert is Braun's home intense pulsed light (IPL) hair-removal line, sold as the Silk·expert Pro 5 and the smaller Silk·expert Mini.[4] People use it on the body and face to cut regrowth over repeated sessions, aiming for smoother skin and less time spent shaving.[4][5]

IPL uses broad-spectrum light that is absorbed by melanin in the hair shaft and heats the follicle; only hairs in the active growth phase respond, so repeated sessions are needed, typically around 8 to 10 spaced 4 to 6 weeks apart in clinic protocols.[2] Braun's own schedule is weekly use for 4 to 12 weeks, then touch-ups.[4] Wikipedia reports that IPL permanently reduces the number of hairs without removing all of them, and that it works best on darker, coarser hair.[2]

Braun builds a skin-tone sensor, the SkinProtect Sensor, into the devices; the company says it reads the skin 80 times a second and adjusts each flash, and that the device flashes only when the skin tone is judged safe.[4] Braun is a Procter & Gamble subsidiary.[1] Studies of IPL exist for clinic devices; no published trial has tested the Silk·expert itself.

angle.text: A home IPL device is used on the face, body or neck to cut down regrowth over repeated sessions, giving a cleaner shaved look with less daily upkeep. The skin-tone sensor is meant to match each flash to the wearer's skin.

paras: Braun lists the Silk·expert Pro 5, with three modes (sensitive, balanced, power), ten energy settings and three attachments, and the Mini, with one balanced mode, three energy settings and no attachments.[4] Braun gives about 10 minutes for a full-body session with the Pro 5 and about 13 with the Mini.[4]
Braun's marketing claims up to 94 percent hair reduction after two years and up to 95 percent in one month, with footnotes that individual results vary.[4] These are manufacturer figures.

T3 reviewed the Pro 5 under the headline of a speedy, powerful and safe way to remove body hair; its UK reviewer reported sparser, finer and slower-growing body hair after about eight months, and described it as best for dark hair with light to mid skin tones.[5]

Wikipedia describes IPL as a handheld xenon flashlamp that emits short, broad-spectrum, non-coherent pulses, roughly in the 400 to 1200 nm range, with filters that block ultraviolet and long infrared light and select the band suited to the target.[2] In hair removal the melanin in the shaft absorbs light and heats the follicle.[2]

Lasers emit coherent single-wavelength light, whereas IPL uses a filtered broad spectrum; IPL is generally regarded as less effective for hair removal than laser, though many patients are satisfied.[2][3]

Braun states that its IPLs are suitable for skin tones I to V and work best on dark hair and fair skin, and that the device flashes only with full skin contact and a skin tone it judges safe.[4] Braun advises against use during pregnancy or lactation, under age 18, and on tattoos, moles or recently tanned skin, and recommends sensitive mode for delicate areas.[4]

A Cleveland Clinic article says home devices suit people with light skin and dark hair, that darker skin carries a risk of burns, and that many home devices include sensors that block use on darker skin.[6] Dermatologist Rachel Ward is quoted there saying home use reduces visible hair over several sessions but is unlikely to be a complete result.[6] The article also advises avoiding the eye area and the genital area.[6]

sections.h: Use for face and body hair
paras: Cleveland Clinic describes home devices being used on areas such as the legs, upper lip and bikini line, with small devices slow for large areas like a full leg.[6] Wikipedia notes that white, grey, red and light blonde hair responds poorly to light-based removal.[3] The earliest facial-hair description in the IPL article is a 1997 report of permanent removal in two beard-treatment patients.[2]

Reported side effects of clinic IPL include redness, burns and pigment changes; contraindications include photosensitising medications and existing skin damage.[2][3] Burns are the main risk, mostly for darker skin, according to Cleveland Clinic.[6]

A 2023 systematic review in Clinical, Cosmetic and Investigational Dermatology found no reported eye injuries from home devices but identified 20 patients with eye damage from office IPL or diode laser devices, about 40 percent of them without eye protection; the authors argued home injuries may be underreported and recommended clear warnings and not bypassing skin-contact sensors.[7]
The FDA defines permanent hair reduction as a long-term, stable reduction in regrowing hairs rather than total removal.[3] Wikipedia notes that rules for these devices vary by jurisdiction.[2]

No studies found of the Braun Silk·expert itself. Studies of clinic IPL are cited by Wikipedia: a 2006 comparison found about 67 percent hair reduction at six months with IPL versus about 69 percent for alexandrite and 72 percent for diode lasers, with temporary side effects in 15.3 percent of IPL patients, and in one trial diode laser reduced hair by 69.2 percent at 12 months versus 52.7 percent for IPL.[2][3] A 2009 study of a second-generation IPL device found 75 percent reduction at four months and up to 80 percent at eight months.[2] These data do not come from Braun devices.
Shimon Eckhouse invented IPL in 1992; ESC Medical commercialised it, and the FDA cleared it for vascular lesions in 1995, pigmented lesions in 1996 and hair removal in 1997.[2]
Braun itself was founded by Max Braun in Frankfurt in 1921, was acquired by Gillette in stages from 1967, and became a Procter & Gamble subsidiary when P&G acquired Gillette in 2005.[1]

card.note: Light-based removal depends on skin tone and hair colour; Braun lists skin tones I to V.

quick.overview:
A home IPL hair-removal device from Braun, sold as the Silk·expert Pro 5 and Mini, with a sensor that reads skin tone before each flash. People use it for smoother skin and less shaving.

Pulsed light is absorbed by hair pigment and heats the follicle. Clinic IPL studies report roughly half to two-thirds hair reduction at six to twelve months; Braun claims higher figures for its own devices.
quick.how: Braun's schedule is weekly use for 4 to 12 weeks with touch-ups after, working across the body in sections; a full-body session takes about 10 minutes with the Pro 5. Users commonly shave first and use it on legs, underarms, bikini line and face.
quick.risks: Redness, burns and pigment changes are reported with IPL, mainly on darker skin. Braun says not to use it during pregnancy, under 18, or on tattoos, moles or tanned skin, and eye injuries from light devices have been reported in clinic settings.
